chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Al-Husayn ibn Saeed, from Al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Yahya ibn Imran al-Halbi, from Abdullah ibn Muskan, from Zurara, who said:

I was in the presence of Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), and with him was a man from the Ansar. A coffin passed by, so the Ansari stood up, but Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) did not stand up. So I remained seated with him (peace be upon him), and the Ansari did not remain standing until they had passed with it, then he sat down. Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said to him: 'What made you stand up?' He said: 'I saw Al-Husayn ibn Ali (peace be upon him) do that.' So Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: 'By Allah, Al-Husayn (peace be upon him) did not do that, nor did anyone from us, the People of the Household, ever stand up for it.' The Ansari said: 'You have cast doubt on me, may Allah rectify you. I thought I had seen him do so.'

key_terms.أَهْلَ الْبَيْتِ: The People of the Household (Ahl al-Bayt)
key_terms.قَامَ: Stood up (as a sign of respect)

ai.seo_question: Did the Imams stand up for funeral processions?
ai.summary: This hadith from Al-Kafi illustrates the distinct fiqh of the Ahl al-Bayt regarding funeral etiquette, where Imam Al-Baqir (AS) clarifies that standing for a coffin is not a practice of the Imams, contrasting with the common custom observed by the Ansari companion. The narrative underscores the importance of adhering to the specific traditions of the Imams rather than general cultural practices, emphasizing that the Ahl al-Bayt's conduct serves as the primary model for religious observance. This correction highlights the scholarly principle that even well-intentioned actions must be validated by the Prophet's household to be considered normative in Shia jurisprudence.
